Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- President Obama should reach out to Iranian opposition leader Mir Hossein Moussavi as tensions in Iran over the disputed presidential elections continue to heighten, a former Bush administration official told CNN Sunday. Paul Wolfowitz was the deputy defense secretary in the Bush administration. "I would certainly find out if he (Moussavi) wants a conversation," former Deputy Defense Secretary Paul Wolfowitz told CNN's Wolf Blitzer. "If he doesn't, I certainly wouldn't push it. But I would make it clear that the phone is an open line." Obama on Saturday issued a written statement on the bloodshed across the streets of Tehran as demonstrators protest the election outcome, saying, "The Iranian government must understand that the world is watching. We mourn each and every innocent life that is lost. "We call on the Iranian government to stop all violent and unjust actions against its own people. The universal rights to assembly and free speech must be respected, and the United States stands with all who seek to exercise those rights." However, Obama has been criticized by some lawmakers and analysts who say he should vocalize a stronger stance on the clashes.  Watch the latest videos being leaked out of Iran » . "I understand the concern about meddling in a way that seems to label the opposition as American tools, but the opposition made it very clear they want support from the world," said Wolfowitz, a staunch supporter of the U.S.-led war in Iraq and a scholar at the American Enterprise Institute. CNN Senior Political Analyst David Gergen added that, "It would be useful for the president to show more forceful leadership internationally on this issue." He noted the graphic images emerging from Iran, including the fatal shooting of a young female protester identified as Neda, saying the violence calls for "some kind of humanity from the West." Gergen and Wolfowitz said the United States should rally with other Western nations and even countries in the region -- including Afghanistan and Turkey, which have recognized incumbent President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad as the winner of the June 12 election -- to support the Iranian people. Ahmadinejad's victory was declared by Iran's election authority, the Guardian Council, spurring massive protests last week, with many demonstrators proclaiming their support for Moussavi. Moussavi and candidate Mehdi Karrubi have rejected the election as fraudulent and demanded a new one. Wolfowitz called Moussavi a "very brave man," saying, "He is resisting. He is putting his life at risk."

WASHINGTON (CNN) — As unrest surrounding Iran’s contested presidential vote intensified, former Bush administration official Paul Wolfowitz said Sunday that President Obama should consider contacting Iranian opposition figure Mir Hossein Moussavi.

Wolfowitz, who served as deputy defense secretary under President George W. Bush, told CNN’s Wolf Blitzer that the administration should first determine whether Moussavi is interested in speaking. If Moussavi declines, Wolfowitz said, Obama should not pressure him, but should make clear that communication remains available.

On Saturday, Obama released a written response to the violence in Tehran, where protesters had taken to the streets to challenge the election results. He said the international community was closely observing the Iranian government’s actions and expressed grief over every innocent person killed. Obama also urged Iranian authorities to end violence and other unjust measures against their citizens, respect the universal freedoms of assembly and expression, and recognize that the United States supports those seeking to exercise those rights.

Some legislators and political analysts, however, criticized Obama for not taking a more forceful public position on the confrontations. Videos of the turmoil continued to emerge from Iran.

Wolfowitz acknowledged concerns that U.S. involvement might allow the Iranian government to portray opposition members as agents of America. Nevertheless, he argued that the opposition had plainly requested international backing. Wolfowitz, an American Enterprise Institute scholar, was a strong advocate of the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq.

CNN senior political analyst David Gergen likewise said the president could provide stronger international leadership on the crisis. Referring to disturbing images coming out of Iran—including footage of a young female protester identified as Neda being fatally shot—Gergen said the bloodshed demanded a humanitarian response from Western countries.

Both Gergen and Wolfowitz urged Washington to coordinate support for the Iranian public with other Western governments and with regional countries. They specifically mentioned Afghanistan and Turkey, even though both had recognized incumbent President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad as the victor in the June 12 election.

Iran’s election authority, the Guardian Council, declared Ahmadinejad the winner. That announcement triggered enormous demonstrations the following week, with many participants openly supporting Moussavi. Moussavi and fellow candidate Mehdi Karrubi denounced the result as fraudulent and called for a new election.

Describing Moussavi as exceptionally courageous, Wolfowitz said the opposition leader was continuing to resist despite putting his own life in danger.

outputs.L4:
Former Deputy Defense Secretary Paul Wolfowitz called on President Barack Obama to establish an open channel of communication with Iranian opposition leader Mir Hossein Moussavi as protests intensified over Iran’s disputed presidential election. Wolfowitz said the United States should make clear that it was prepared to listen to Moussavi and other opposition figures, while taking care not to give the Iranian government an excuse to depict the protest movement as an American operation.

Wolfowitz argued that the worsening violence required a stronger response from Washington and its allies. Images of demonstrators being beaten, arrested, and killed had spread around the world, fueling international outrage. Particular attention focused on the death of a young woman identified as Neda, whose final moments were captured on video after she was shot during the unrest. Her death became a symbol of the government’s crackdown and of the risks being taken by protesters demanding political accountability.

Political analyst David Gergen likewise urged more coordinated Western leadership. He said the United States should work with European governments and other democratic allies to present a united front, publicly condemning the violence and supporting Iranians’ rights to peaceful assembly, free expression, and a credible electoral process. A broad international response, he suggested, would be harder for Tehran to dismiss as unilateral American interference.

Both men acknowledged the central dilemma facing the Obama administration. Forceful American involvement could help draw attention to abuses and reassure protesters that they were not alone, but it could also allow Iranian authorities to accuse Moussavi and his supporters of acting on behalf of Washington. For that reason, they advocated carefully calibrated support rather than direct intervention.

Their comments reflected growing pressure on Obama to move beyond cautious statements as the crackdown escalated. Wolfowitz and Gergen maintained that the United States and its partners should neither attempt to control Iran’s opposition movement nor remain silent in the face of violence. Instead, they argued, Western governments should communicate with opposition leaders, defend universal democratic rights, document abuses, and coordinate their public and diplomatic response while allowing the movement to retain its independent, Iranian character.

# Wolfowitz urges Obama to contact Iranian opposition leader

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Former Deputy Defense Secretary Paul Wolfowitz urged President Barack Obama to contact Iranian opposition leader Mir Hossein Mousavi as protests continued over Iran’s disputed 2009 presidential election.

Wolfowitz said direct outreach would demonstrate American support for Iranians demanding that their votes be counted, while giving Mousavi an opportunity to indicate what kind of international response would be most helpful.

Mousavi, a former prime minister, challenged the official results declaring President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad the overwhelming winner of the June 12 election. Mousavi’s supporters alleged widespread fraud and poured into the streets of Tehran and other cities, prompting a forceful response from Iranian authorities.

The Obama administration initially reacted cautiously, condemning violence and calling for the will of the Iranian people to be respected without explicitly endorsing Mousavi. Obama argued that overt U.S. involvement could allow Iran’s leaders to portray the demonstrations as a foreign-backed movement.

Wolfowitz, who served in the George W. Bush administration and was a prominent advocate of the 2003 invasion of Iraq, said that concern should not prevent the president from speaking directly with the opposition leader.

The former Pentagon official argued that Washington should avoid dictating events inside Iran but should make clear that it stands with peaceful protesters and supports demands for a credible electoral process.

Iranian leaders accused the United States and other Western governments of interfering in the country’s internal affairs. Mousavi and other opposition figures rejected claims that the protest movement was directed from abroad.

The unrest became the most serious domestic challenge to Iran’s clerical establishment in years. Images of mass demonstrations, clashes with security forces and the death of protester Neda Agha-Soltan drew international attention despite restrictions on journalists and communications.

Obama later sharpened his criticism of Tehran, saying the United States was “appalled and outraged” by the Iranian government’s crackdown. But the administration stopped short of establishing a public alliance with Mousavi, maintaining that Iran’s political future should be decided by Iranians.

counterfactuals.output:
### Criticism of Obama’s response to Iran’s 2009 election crisis

Following Iran’s disputed June 12, 2009 presidential election, President Barack Obama was criticized for responding too cautiously as security forces attacked demonstrators protesting the announced reelection of Mahmoud Ahmadinejad.

Obama initially said he was “deeply troubled” by the violence and urged Iranian authorities to respect peaceful dissent. However, he avoided endorsing opposition candidate Mir Hossein Mousavi or declaring the election fraudulent. He argued that the United States should not become the central issue in an internal Iranian struggle, noting that overt American involvement could allow Tehran to portray protesters as agents of Washington. His administration also hoped to preserve the possibility of negotiations over Iran’s nuclear program.

Critics said this caution risked appearing indifferent to democratic protesters:

- **Paul Wolfowitz**, former deputy defense secretary under George W. Bush, argued that Obama’s position amounted to an abdication of American moral leadership. In a Washington Post commentary, Wolfowitz said the United States should make unmistakably clear that it stood with Iranians demanding political freedom. He contended that expressions of support would not constitute improper intervention and that silence or excessive restraint could demoralize demonstrators while encouraging the regime.

- **David Gergen**, a presidential adviser in several administrations and a CNN analyst, described Obama’s early language as too muted. Although Gergen acknowledged the danger that forceful American rhetoric could be exploited by Iran’s leaders, he said the escalating repression created a need for the president to speak more clearly and firmly in defense of peaceful protest and human rights. His criticism was more measured than Wolfowitz’s: he accepted the rationale for initial caution but argued that events increasingly required stronger presidential leadership.

Other critics, including Republicans in Congress and some democracy advocates, similarly pressed Obama to condemn the crackdown more directly. Senator John McCain, for example, urged him to speak out more forcefully on behalf of the protesters.

As violence intensified—and particularly after images of the fatal shooting of protester Neda Agha-Soltan circulated worldwide—Obama sharpened his language. On June 23, he said the United States was “appalled and outraged” by the threats, beatings, imprisonments and killings, and declared that Iran’s government had to respect the universal rights of assembly and free expression.

The dispute therefore centered less on whether Obama opposed the repression than on tactics: his critics emphasized America’s obligation to offer clear moral support, while the administration feared that an overtly interventionist posture would strengthen the Iranian government’s claim that the unrest was foreign-directed and might undermine the protesters themselves.

**BREAKING NEWS | June 23, 2009**

# Obama Condemns Iran Bloodshed as Pressure Grows for Stronger Western Support

**WASHINGTON/TEHRAN** — President Barack Obama on Tuesday sharpened his response to Iran’s disputed presidential election, saying the United States was “appalled and outraged” by the violence against demonstrators and condemning efforts to suppress peaceful dissent.

“The United States and the international community have been appalled and outraged by the threats, the beatings and imprisonments of the last few days,” Obama said at the White House. He added that the Iranian government “must understand that the world is watching.”

Iran has faced nearly two weeks of unrest since officials declared President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad the winner of the June 12 election over opposition candidate Mir Hossein Mousavi. Mousavi’s supporters allege widespread fraud and have taken to the streets in demonstrations not seen since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

Authorities have restricted foreign media, disrupted internet and mobile-phone services, and deployed police and pro-government militia units against protesters. Images recorded by witnesses—including video of the fatal shooting of a young woman identified as Neda Agha-Soltan—have circulated worldwide and intensified criticism of the crackdown.

Obama had initially used restrained language, saying Washington did not want to become a pretext for Iranian leaders to dismiss the protests as foreign interference. But critics in the United States and Europe have urged Western governments to offer clearer moral support to the demonstrators.

Republican lawmakers and some human-rights advocates said the administration should more forcefully denounce Tehran, demand the release of detained activists and journalists, and coordinate international pressure against officials responsible for violence.

The White House maintained that stronger rhetoric must not allow Iran’s leaders to portray an internal political crisis as one directed from abroad. Obama said it was for Iranians—not the United States—to choose Iran’s leadership, while insisting that universal rights to peaceful assembly and free expression must be respected.

Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, has backed the official result and warned protesters to leave the streets. Opposition leaders have continued to challenge the count despite arrests, threats and a widening security crackdown.

With independent reporting inside Iran severely limited, the full number of casualties and detentions remains unclear. Protesters continued using social media and amateur video to document events, turning the election crisis into an early test of digital activism—and of how far Western governments are willing to go in supporting a popular uprising without appearing to control it.

**WASHINGTON (CNN) —** Former Deputy Defense Secretary Paul Wolfowitz said the United States should look for ways to communicate with Iranian opposition leader Mir Hossein Moussavi while building international pressure on Tehran over its disputed presidential election and crackdown on demonstrators.

In an interview with CNN’s Wolf Blitzer, Wolfowitz argued that Washington should support Iranians challenging the election results without taking steps that would allow the government to portray the protests as an American operation.

He said any contact with Moussavi would need to be handled carefully and, if possible, privately. The United States should determine what assistance opposition figures want rather than publicly embracing them in a way that could undermine their standing inside Iran, he said.

Wolfowitz also urged the Obama administration to rally allies and other governments behind a strong response, saying broad international condemnation would be more effective than unilateral U.S. pressure. He called for Washington to press European nations and other major powers to denounce violence against protesters and demand respect for the Iranian people’s political rights.

The former Pentagon official said President Barack Obama’s initial caution was understandable but argued that the United States should speak more forcefully as reports emerged of arrests, bloodshed and restrictions on communications.

The challenge for Washington, Wolfowitz said, is to make clear that it stands with Iranians seeking a fair political process while denying Tehran’s leaders an opportunity to blame the unrest on foreign interference.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed CNN report on the aftermath of Mahmoud Ahmadinejad’s disputed re-election, mentioning Moussavi, Mehdi Karrubi, the death of Neda, Obama’s response, and recommendations from Wolfowitz and Gergen.
counterfactuals.output:
## Iran reels after Ahmadinejad’s disputed re-election

**TEHRAN, Iran —** The disputed re-election of Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad in June 2009 triggered the country’s largest demonstrations since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, exposing deep political divisions and prompting a violent government crackdown watched around the world.

Iranian authorities declared Ahmadinejad the winner of the June 12 election with nearly 63% of the vote, compared with about 34% for his principal challenger, former Prime Minister **Mir-Hossein Moussavi**. The speed of the count and Ahmadinejad’s unexpectedly wide margin immediately generated allegations of fraud.

Moussavi rejected the official result and called for the election to be annulled. His supporters, many wearing green campaign colors, flooded the streets of Tehran and other cities. “Where is my vote?” became the defining slogan of what came to be known as the **Green Movement**.

Another reformist candidate, former parliamentary speaker **Mehdi Karrubi**, also challenged the result. Karrubi later became one of the most outspoken critics of the security forces, publicizing allegations that detainees had been beaten, tortured and sexually abused. Iranian officials denied systematic mistreatment and accused opposition leaders of encouraging unrest.

### Demonstrations and crackdown

For several days, enormous crowds marched through Tehran, sometimes in silence. Authorities restricted foreign journalists, disrupted mobile-phone service and blocked or slowed access to social-media sites. Protesters nevertheless used online videos, photographs and eyewitness accounts to document events.

Security forces, riot police and members of the pro-government Basij militia confronted demonstrators with batons, tear gas and, in some cases, gunfire. Opposition figures, journalists, students and activists were arrested. The government blamed foreign governments and international media organizations for helping foment what it described as a foreign-backed uprising.

Supreme Leader **Ayatollah Ali Khamenei**, who holds ultimate authority in Iran, endorsed the official election result. In a June 19 sermon, he warned demonstrators to leave the streets and said opposition leaders would be responsible for further bloodshed. The Guardian Council later conducted a limited review and upheld Ahmadinejad’s victory, rejecting demands for a new election.

### The death of Neda

The crisis acquired a human face on June 20, when **Neda Agha-Soltan**, a 26-year-old woman, was fatally shot near an anti-government demonstration in Tehran. A graphic cellphone video showed her collapsing as bystanders tried to save her.

The footage spread rapidly online, turning Neda into an international symbol of the protest movement and of the costs of the crackdown. Opposition supporters blamed pro-government forces, while Iranian authorities offered conflicting accounts and questioned who was responsible. The precise circumstances remained contested, but the emotional impact of the images was immediate and global.

President Barack Obama said the video was “heartbreaking” and called the violence “fundamentally unjust.” He later said Neda’s death had demonstrated the brutality taking place and that her loss had become a powerful symbol.

### Obama’s cautious response

The Obama administration initially responded carefully. The president said the United States should not become a political “football” in Iran’s internal struggle and stressed that the future of the country had to be decided by Iranians themselves.

That caution reflected a long history of mistrust, including the CIA-supported overthrow of Iranian Prime Minister Mohammad Mossadegh in 1953 and decades of hostile relations after the Islamic Revolution. White House officials feared that an overt American endorsement of Moussavi could allow Iranian leaders to discredit the protesters as agents of Washington.

As the crackdown intensified, however, Obama’s language became firmer. He condemned the violence, defended the rights of Iranians to peaceful assembly and free expression, and said the world was watching. He also rejected suggestions that concerns over human rights should be subordinated to negotiations over Iran’s nuclear program.

Obama stopped short of calling for regime change or directly endorsing Moussavi. His position was that Washington should support universal rights without claiming ownership of a movement whose legitimacy came from within Iran.

### Wolfowitz urges stronger backing

Former Deputy Defense Secretary **Paul Wolfowitz** argued that Obama’s early reaction was too restrained. Wolfowitz urged the administration to give clearer moral and political support to Iranians demanding that their votes be counted and their rights respected.

His recommendations centered on using the American presidency’s platform to:

- Condemn repression unequivocally.
- Demand the release of peaceful protesters and opposition activists.
- Press for access by journalists and human-rights monitors.
- Refuse to treat the official election result as unquestionably legitimate.
- Coordinate international pressure without implying that the United States controlled the opposition movement.

Wolfowitz’s argument was not principally for American military intervention. Rather, he maintained that strong presidential rhetoric and diplomatic pressure could help protect dissidents, reduce their isolation and signal to Iranian officials that abuses would carry international consequences.

### Gergen calls for moral clarity without making America the story

CNN senior political analyst **David Gergen** also said Obama needed to express stronger support for democratic rights, particularly after the killing of Neda and the escalation of the crackdown. At the same time, Gergen emphasized that the president had to avoid allowing Iran’s leadership to portray the demonstrations as an American project.

Gergen’s recommended approach was calibrated: Obama should speak with greater moral clarity, stand publicly with those seeking peaceful change and rally other democracies, but avoid operational involvement or rhetoric suggesting that Washington was directing the protests.

In effect, Gergen argued that silence could be interpreted as abandonment, while excessive intervention could undermine the very people the United States hoped to support. The challenge was to keep the focus on Iranian citizens and the conduct of their government.

### Lasting consequences

Ahmadinejad was inaugurated for a second term, but the election crisis damaged the government’s legitimacy among many Iranians. Moussavi and Karrubi remained symbols of opposition and were later placed under house arrest, beginning in 2011.

The Green Movement did not remove Iran’s leadership, but it revealed substantial dissatisfaction with the political system and demonstrated the growing power of citizen-recorded images and social media. Neda’s death became the most enduring symbol of the uprising, while the debate over Obama’s response highlighted a recurring dilemma in American foreign policy: how to support democratic movements abroad without discrediting them through the appearance of U.S. control.
